title: Perry's Black Ships
text:
For more than two centuries Tokugawa Japan had strictly limited contact with the outside world, allowing only Dutch and Chinese traders at Nagasaki. Foreign ships that tried to open relations had been turned away.

In July 1853 Commodore Matthew Perry of the United States Navy sailed into Edo Bay with four warships, two of them steam frigates belching black smoke. The Japanese called them the black ships. Perry refused orders to go to Nagasaki. He insisted on delivering a letter from President Millard Fillmore asking for trade, coaling stations and protection for shipwrecked sailors, and he made clear that he would deliver it in person or by force if necessary. Japanese officials received the letter at Kurihama. Perry announced that he would return the next year for an answer and sailed away.

The shogunate was divided and alarmed. Its coastal defenses were no match for the guns of steam warships, and it knew what had happened to China in the Opium War. It took the unusual step of consulting the daimyo, which weakened its authority.

Perry came back in February 1854 with a larger squadron. He brought gifts including a miniature steam railway and a telegraph. On 31 March 1854 the Treaty of Kanagawa was signed, opening the ports of Shimoda and Hakodate to American ships. No shots had been fired, but the episode set off the crisis that ended the shogunate fourteen years later.
lesson: A credible display of strength, combined with clear demands and time to think, can bring an opponent to the table without a fight. It may also unsettle more than you intended.
people: Matthew C. Perry, Tokugawa shogunate, Abe Masahiro
source: Narrative of the Expedition of an American Squadron to the China Seas and Japan (1856), compiled under Perry's supervision
